facts.statement: The genus Igdamanosaurus was named by Lingham-Soliar in 1991.
Igdamanosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian stage.
The single known species, Igdamanosaurus aegyptiacus, lived in marine environments in Africa during the Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: from Maastrichtian-aged marine environments of Africa

facts.statement: Fossils of Igdamanosaurus have been found in the Duwi Formation of Egypt and the Dukamaje Formation of Niger.
facts.quote: Its fragmentary fossil remains have been recovered from the Duwi Formation of Egypt and the Dukamaje Formation of Niger.

facts.statement: Igdamanosaurus belongs to the Globidensini tribe and is recognized by its rounded, knob-like teeth.
facts.quote: It is classified as part of the Globidensini tribe (within the Mosasaurinae), and is like the other members of the tribe recognised by its rounded and knob-like teeth.

facts.statement: The specialized teeth of Igdamanosaurus suggest it had a durophagous diet, likely crushing hard-shelled prey.
facts.quote: These teeth indicate a highly specialized lifestyle, likely including a durophagous diet.

facts.statement: Igdamanosaurus was a small mosasaur roughly the size of its relative Carinodens.
facts.quote: Igdamanosaurus was a small durophagous mosasaur at a size roughly similar to the closely related globidensin Carinodens.

facts.statement: Igdamanosaurus used its teeth to crush armored prey such as molluscs and turtles instead of typical fish or reptile prey.
facts.quote: These teeth were better suited for crushing armored prey like molluscs and turtles, rather than fish or other reptiles normally preyed on by other mosasaurs.

facts.statement: Igdamanosaurus possessed a dentary of massive proportions similar to those of Globidens and Prognathodon.
facts.quote: The dentary is noted as being of massive proportions, similar to the massive and robust dentaries found in Globidens and Prognathodon.

facts.statement: The teeth of Igdamanosaurus were straight, broad cones with rounded, domed tips and a subcircular cross-section.
facts.quote: The teeth are straight, broad cones with rounded and domed tips. In cross-section the teeth are subcircular.

facts.statement: Each tooth of Igdamanosaurus had an unwaisted base covered in approximately 65 to 70 fine parallel ridges.
facts.quote: Tooth crowns possess unwaisted bases and are covered in fine parallel ribbing or striae, numbering at approximately 65 to 70 per tooth.

facts.statement: The largest preserved tooth of Igdamanosaurus measured approximately 27 mm in height and 22 mm in width.
facts.quote: the largest one measures approximately 27 mm high and 22 mm wide.

facts.statement: The species was originally named Globidens aegyptiacus by Zdansky in 1935 before being moved to its own genus by Lingham-Soliar in 1991.
facts.quote: Originally named as Globidens aegyptiacus by Otto Zdansky (1935), the species was first recognised as sufficiently distinct to be separated into its own genus by Lingham-Soliar (1991)

facts.statement: Lingham-Soliar (1991) classified Igdamanosaurus within the Plioplatecarpinae based on vertical striae suggesting a Platecarpus-like ancestor.
facts.quote: Lingham-Soliar (1991) noted that the vertical striae present in Igdamanosaurus would suggest that it represented a completely new type of durophagous mosasaur that was derived from a Platecarpus-like ancestor rather than a Clidastes-like one and thus classified it as part of the Plioplatecarpinae.

facts.statement: Recent analyses place Igdamanosaurus within the Mosasaurinae tribe Globidensini as a relative of Carinodens and Globidens.
facts.quote: The latest analyses all place Igdamanosaurus within the Mosasaurinae however, within the Globidensini tribe as a close relative of Carinodens and Globidens, or even an indeterminate species of Globidens.

facts.statement: Igdamanosaurus is classified as a member of the subfamily Mosasaurinae.
Igdamanosaurus belongs to the family Mosasauridae.
Igdamanosaurus is classified as a reptile.
The time range for Igdamanosaurus is estimated from 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)
